Beldia keeps the guards at their posts and turns his attention to the mediator's terms. The silence is welcome, but accepting it as an apology would give the workers too easy an escape from the damage.

“So they do know how to stop. Good. We will discuss repairs, and I will inspect what they restore before I call this finished.”

He offers a limited agreement rather than dismissing the grievance. Monitoring gives him something more useful than another noisy confrontation: a way to insist that the cessation continues. He does not promise friendship or forgive the earlier attacks. If the workers resume, he makes clear that he will reopen the demand.

Beldia interrupts the proposed agreement and gestures toward his guards. Words about cessation sound like another insult while the damaging noise continues.

“You offer me an end to this while they are still doing it? Tell them to stop now. Until then, your agreement is only more noise.”

He orders the guards to prepare to halt the workers' activity, without claiming they have already obeyed. His next demand becomes punitive: the workers must answer for continuing after his complaint, as well as repair the damage. The mediator may still obtain a bargain, but Beldia now wants a visible concession before discussing terms. His anger gives him a reason to threaten, not a guarantee that the threat will work.

Beldia adjusts the position of his head to study the priest and keeps his body ready rather than rushing forward. The twinge gives him little reason to abandon the gate, although it tells him nothing certain about a second spell.

“Was that your greeting, or did you expect me to disappear? State your business before you try another.”

His voice remains dismissive, and he is tempted to treat the first result as a measure of the whole opponent. He nevertheless watches for the next movement. The armor has endured this attack; it has not revealed the priest's level or every ability. He gives no ground yet, but seeks an answer before committing himself.

Beldia moves aside from the position where the spell struck and checks his armor while trying to keep the priest in view. The surviving protection matters, but the pain has spoiled his easy estimate of the encounter.

“What level are you? Do not tell me that was an ordinary beginner's greeting.”

He tries to recover an authoritative tone, then waits rather than immediately closing the distance. A second cast might expose a limit he does not understand. He can still threaten or fight, but he wants information before relying on the armor again. His stagger is neither purification nor proof of inevitable defeat; it is an unwelcome reason to reconsider how cheaply he expected to win.

He studies the proposed statement and agrees to its face-saving language, while making the key's return part of the same exchange.

“Both parties stood their ground. We end the dispute as a draw, and the archive returns to my access. That is the statement I will make.”

He dislikes depending on the rival, but this wording lets him recover the practical object without publicly accepting inferiority. He does not call the rival a friend or apologize for unspecified conduct. Before speaking to the witnesses, he asks the rival to confirm that the offered return follows immediately. The confirmation is a request, not a completed handover; if the terms change, he intends to bargain again.

He refuses the proposed wording before attempting another bargain. The key cannot be taken by force, but that does not make public humiliation an attractive price.

“You want an end to the dispute, or an audience for an insult? Say that neither party prevailed and that access is restored. I will make that statement.”

He keeps his attention on the actual exchange instead of pretending he can recover the archive through a threat alone. Dependence makes his language more controlled than he would like. If the rival insists, he will have to weigh the archive against the insult; he has not resolved that choice yet. For now, he offers a replacement that preserves his standing.
